questions.q: 1 a) List and define the conditions that critical section problem must satisfy. [L1][CO3] [2M]
questions.a: A solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three conditions: (1) Mutual Exclusion — if one process is executing in its critical section, no other process may be executing in its critical section. (2) Progress — if no process is in its critical section and some processes wish to enter, only those not in their remainder section may participate in deciding which one enters next, and this decision cannot be postponed indefinitely. (3) Bounded Waiting — after a process requests entry, there is a bound on the number of times other processes may enter their critical sections before that request is granted. It is also assumed that each process executes at nonzero speed and that no assumption is made about relative process speeds or the number of CPUs.
questions.explanation: These are the three classic requirements (mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting) that any valid critical-section protocol must meet.
questions.oneShotPreview: 3 conditions: Mutual Exclusion (only one in CS), Progress (decision not deferred), Bounded Waiting (no indefinite starvation).

questions.q: 1 b) Give the benefits and drawbacks of Mutex Locks. [L1][CO3] [2M]
questions.a: A mutex lock is a synchronization tool that enforces mutual exclusion: a process must acquire() the lock before entering a critical section and release() it on exit, and acquire() blocks or spins while the lock is held by another. Benefits: simple to understand and implement, directly supported by hardware atomic instructions (test-and-set/compare-and-swap), reliably guarantee mutual exclusion, and are efficient for short critical sections in kernel and user code. Drawbacks: spinlock versions waste CPU cycles through busy-waiting, blocking versions incur context-switch overhead, they provide no guaranteed bounded waiting (a thread can starve), they can cause deadlock if a holder fails to release or locks are taken in inconsistent order, and they are vulnerable to priority inversion. Forgetting to release a mutex can leave it permanently unavailable.
questions.explanation: Mutex locks trade simplicity and hardware support for risks such as busy-waiting, starvation, deadlock and priority inversion.
questions.oneShotPreview: Mutex = acquire/release lock; benefits: simple, hardware-friendly, reliable; drawbacks: busy-wait, starvation, deadlock, priority inversion.

questions.q: 1 c) What is Resource-Allocation Graphs? List its properties. [L1][CO5] [2M]
questions.a: A resource-allocation graph (RAG) is a directed graph used to model the state of a system for deadlock detection. Nodes are of two types: process nodes Pi (circles) and resource-type nodes Rj (rectangles, with dots representing individual instances). Edges are Pi -> Rj, a request edge (process is requesting an instance), and Rj -> Pi, an assignment edge (an instance is currently allocated to the process). Properties: (1) a request edge is converted to an assignment edge when the request is granted and back when the resource is released; (2) if the graph has no cycles, no process is deadlocked; (3) if every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle is a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock; (4) if multiple instances exist, a cycle is only a necessary (not sufficient) condition — deadlock occurs only when every process in the cycle is blocked on a resource held by another member of the cycle.
questions.explanation: The RAG is the standard deadlock-detection model; the meaning of a cycle depends on whether resource types have single or multiple instances.
questions.oneShotPreview: RAG: circles=processes, rectangles=resources; request/assignment edges; cycle => deadlock only if single-instance (else necessary, not sufficient).

questions.q: 1 d) Describe Deadlock and the methods to handling them. [L1][CO5] [2M]
questions.a: Deadlock is a state in which a set of processes is permanently blocked because each holds at least one resource and is waiting to acquire another resource held by another process in the set, so none can proceed. It can occur only when all four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. The methods for handling deadlocks are: (1) Deadlock prevention — design the system so at least one of the four conditions cannot hold (e.g., request all resources at once, allow preemption, impose resource ordering). (2) Deadlock avoidance — use runtime information such as the Banker's algorithm to keep the system out of unsafe states. (3) Deadlock detection and recovery — allow deadlocks, detect them with a resource-allocation/wait-for graph or detection algorithm, then recover by terminating processes or preempting resources. (4) Ignore the problem (ostrich algorithm) — assume deadlocks are rare, as most general-purpose OSes do.
questions.explanation: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions, and the four handling strategies range from structural prevention to simply ignoring the issue.
questions.oneShotPreview: Deadlock = cycle of processes holding & waiting; 4 Coffman conditions. Handle via prevention, avoidance (Banker's), detection+recovery, or ignore.

questions.q: 1 e) Give the difference between deadlock and starvation. [L4][CO5] [2M]
questions.a: Deadlock is a state in which a group of processes are each blocked waiting for resources held by one another in a closed cycle, so none of them can ever make progress without external intervention. Starvation (indefinite blocking) is a state in which a single process is perpetually denied the resource or CPU time it needs because other processes are always favored, although the system as a whole continues to make progress. In deadlock there is a genuine circular wait and no process progresses; in starvation there is no cycle — only unfair allocation that repeatedly overlooks one waiting process. Deadlock can be detected by a cycle in a wait-for graph, whereas starvation is prevented by fairness mechanisms such as aging or fair scheduling.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is a circular wait with zero progress (deadlock) versus unfair allocation where others keep progressing (starvation).
questions.oneShotPreview: Deadlock = circular wait, nobody progresses; starvation = one process perpetually skipped while others progress (fix: aging).

questions.q: 2 a) What is critical section problem? Explain with example. [L2][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: The critical-section problem is the challenge of designing a protocol so that cooperating processes do not concurrently execute the part of their code (the critical section) that accesses and modifies shared data, which could otherwise corrupt it. A correct solution must guarantee mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Example: two processes P1 and P2 both increment a shared variable counter with the statement counter++. If both read the value 5 and then both write back 6, the final value is 6 instead of the correct 7 — a race condition caused by interleaved read-modify-write operations. A synchronization tool such as a mutex lock or Peterson's solution ensures only one process at a time executes the critical section, so no increment is lost.
questions.explanation: The counter++ interleaving is the textbook example of a race condition that the critical-section protocol must prevent.
questions.oneShotPreview: Critical-section problem: protect shared data updates; e.g., two processes doing counter++ can lose an increment (race) — need mutual exclusion.

questions.q: 2 b) Describe deadlock recovery and how it is performed. [L2][CO5] [5M]
questions.a: Deadlock recovery is the phase carried out after a deadlock has been detected, in which the system breaks the circular wait so that processes can proceed. Two main approaches exist: (1) Process termination — either abort all deadlocked processes (simple but drastic, discarding all their work) or abort one process at a time until the cycle is broken (less destructive but requires repeated detection). The victim is chosen using criteria such as least work done, fewest resources held, lowest priority cost, and least CPU time consumed. (2) Resource preemption — select a victim and take away some of its resources, give them to a blocked process to break the cycle, then roll the victim back to a previously saved safe checkpoint and restart it. A cost-based preemption scheme with rollback (and aging) is used to avoid repeatedly preempting the same process and to prevent starvation.
questions.explanation: Recovery breaks the cycle either by killing deadlocked processes or by preempting resources from a victim and rolling it back, with victim choice minimizing cost.
questions.oneShotPreview: Recovery: abort all/one deadlocked process (pick victim by cost) or preempt resources + roll back victim to break the cycle.

questions.q: 3 Define process synchronization and explain Peterson solution algorithms. [L2][CO3] [10M]
questions.a: Process synchronization is the coordination of the execution order of cooperating processes so that they can safely share data and resources and avoid race conditions, by ensuring mutually exclusive access to critical sections. Peterson's solution is a classical software-based algorithm for two processes, P0 and P1, using two shared variables: int turn and boolean flag[2]. A process Pi sets flag[i] = true (announcing interest) and turn = j (yielding priority to the other), then waits in the loop while (flag[j] && turn == j); when it exits the loop it enters the critical section, and on exit sets flag[i] = false. Mutual exclusion holds because both processes cannot simultaneously have their flag true with the turn favoring themselves; progress and bounded waiting are satisfied because the turn variable alternates priority, so neither waits indefinitely. It assumes atomic reads and writes and is limited to two processes, but it elegantly satisfies all three critical-section requirements without hardware lock instructions.
questions.explanation: Peterson's algorithm uses flags plus the turn variable to satisfy all three critical-section requirements for two processes, though its atomicity assumption and two-process limit restrict practical use.
questions.oneShotPreview: Sync = coordinate processes to avoid races. Peterson (2 proc): flag[i]=true, turn=j, wait while flag[j]&&turn==j; satisfies all 3 conditions.

questions.q: 4 Discuss in detail about the hardware-based solution for synchronization. [L2][CO3] [10M]
questions.a: Hardware-based synchronization uses special atomic machine instructions to achieve mutual exclusion without complex software protocols. (1) Disabling interrupts: on a single-CPU system a process disables interrupts while in its critical section so no context switch can occur; it is simple but fails on multiprocessors and grants user processes dangerous power. (2) Test-and-Set (TSL): an atomic instruction that reads a memory word and sets it to true in one indivisible operation; a shared boolean lock is repeatedly tested until the old value is false, then the lock is held and cleared on exit. (3) Compare-and-Swap (CAS): atomically compares a memory word with an expected value and writes a new value only if they match, returning the old value; widely used in modern lock implementations. (4) Swap/XCHG: atomically exchanges the contents of two words. These primitives implement spinlocks (busy-wait locks) and underpin higher-level tools such as mutexes and semaphores. They work on multiple CPUs but busy-waiting wastes CPU cycles and can cause starvation and priority inversion.
questions.explanation: Atomic hardware instructions make the read-modify-write indivisible, which is the foundation of all hardware locks and higher-level synchronization tools.
questions.oneShotPreview: Hardware sync: disable interrupts (uni-CPU), Test-and-Set, Compare-and-Swap, Swap -> atomic read-modify-write -> spinlocks; fast but busy-waits.

questions.q: 5 What are Mutex Locks? List its Components and analyze the different types with example. [L4][CO3] [10M]
questions.a: A mutex lock (mutual exclusion lock) is the simplest synchronization tool: it is a lock variable that a process must acquire before entering a critical section and release afterward, so that only one process holds it at a time and others block or spin. Its components are a lock variable/flag (available or acquired), an acquire() operation that atomically tests and sets the lock (waiting if unavailable), and a release() operation that atomically clears the lock and hands it to a waiter. Types: (1) Spinlock (busy-wait mutex) — the process repeatedly polls the lock using atomic test-and-set; suitable for very short critical sections on multiprocessors, e.g., short kernel locks, but wastes CPU. (2) Blocking/sleeping mutex — a failed acquire puts the thread to sleep and the OS wakes it on release, avoiding CPU waste at the cost of context switches, e.g., pthread_mutex_t. (3) Recursive/reentrant mutex — may be re-acquired multiple times by the same thread. (4) A binary semaphore acts as a mutex. Example: pthread_mutex_lock(&m); counter++; pthread_mutex_unlock(&m); prevents lost updates on a shared counter.
questions.explanation: Mutex types differ mainly in how a failed acquire is handled (spin vs sleep), trading CPU idling for context-switch cost; the components are the lock variable plus atomic acquire/release.
questions.oneShotPreview: Mutex = lock with acquire()/release(); types: spinlock (busy-wait, short CS), blocking mutex (sleep/wake), recursive; e.g., pthread_mutex protecting counter++.

questions.q: 6 a) What is Semaphore? Explain its types with example. [L2][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: A semaphore is an integer synchronization variable that, apart from initialization, is accessed only through two atomic operations: wait() (also called P, down, or acquire), which decrements the value and blocks the calling process if the result is negative, and signal() (V, up, or release), which increments the value and wakes a waiting process. Types: (1) Binary semaphore — the value is restricted to 0 or 1; it is used for mutual exclusion and behaves like a mutex. (2) Counting semaphore — the value may range over any integer and is used to control access to a finite number of identical resources, initialized to the number available. (Some texts also distinguish strong/weak semaphores.) Example: a binary semaphore S initialized to 1 protects a critical section via wait(S); critical_section; signal(S); while counting semaphores empty = n and full = 0 coordinate a producer and consumer over an n-slot buffer.
questions.explanation: Semaphores generalize locks through an integer count; wait/signal are atomic, and binary versus counting determines whether they enforce mutual exclusion or resource counting.
questions.oneShotPreview: Semaphore = int with atomic wait(P)/signal(V); binary (0/1 mutex) vs counting (resource count); e.g., S=1 guards CS, empty/full for producer-consumer.

questions.q: 6 b) Explain producer consumer problem using semaphore. [L2][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: The producer-consumer problem has a producer that generates items into a buffer of size n and a consumer that removes them; the producer must not write to a full buffer, the consumer must not read from an empty one, and access must be mutually exclusive. The semaphore solution uses three semaphores: mutex = 1 (binary, for exclusive buffer access), empty = n (number of free slots), and full = 0 (number of occupied slots). Producer: produce item; wait(empty); wait(mutex); insert item into buffer; signal(mutex); signal(full). Consumer: wait(full); wait(mutex); remove item; signal(mutex); signal(empty); consume item. The empty and full semaphores enforce the capacity constraints, while mutex prevents simultaneous modification of the buffer. The order of the two waits matters — taking mutex before empty/full can deadlock — while the two signals may be in any order.
questions.explanation: empty/full enforce the buffer capacity bounds and mutex serializes the shared buffer, so no busy-waiting or race occurs; the wait order avoids deadlock.
questions.oneShotPreview: Producer-consumer: empty=n, full=0, mutex=1; producer wait(empty)->wait(mutex)->add->signal(mutex)->signal(full); consumer reverse.

questions.q: 7 a) Describe how monitor achieve process synchronization. Also, mention its advantages and disadvantages. [L2][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: A monitor is a high-level, language-level synchronization construct that encapsulates shared data together with the procedures that operate on it, and provides an implicit lock ensuring that only one process/thread can be active inside the monitor at a time. Processes enter the monitor by calling one of its procedures, so mutual exclusion is automatic. Condition variables support condition-based blocking through wait(c) and signal(c): wait(c) releases the monitor lock and suspends the caller, while signal(c) wakes a process waiting on that condition. Advantages: easier and safer than semaphores because the compiler/language enforces mutual exclusion, reducing errors such as wrong wait order or a forgotten signal; more readable and maintainable; no busy-waiting. Disadvantages: requires language/compiler support (not native in C/C++), is less flexible than semaphores for some problems, any process inside the monitor blocks all others, and correct condition-variable semantics (signal-and-wait vs signal-and-continue) are subtle.
questions.explanation: Monitors move the correctness burden from the programmer to the language by combining shared data, procedures, an implicit lock, and condition variables.
questions.oneShotPreview: Monitor = shared data + procedures + implicit lock + condition variables (wait/signal); safer than semaphores but language-supported & less flexible.

questions.q: 7 b) Discuss in detail about the Reader and Writer Problem using semaphore [L2][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: The readers-writers problem concerns a shared database in which reader processes only read data and writer processes modify it; many readers may read concurrently, but a writer requires exclusive access with no readers and no other writers. The classic reader-preference semaphore solution uses mutex = 1 to protect the shared counter readcount and wrt = 1 to lock the database against writers. Reader: wait(mutex); readcount++; if (readcount == 1) wait(wrt); signal(mutex); perform read; wait(mutex); readcount--; if (readcount == 0) signal(wrt); signal(mutex). Writer: wait(wrt); perform write; signal(wrt). The first reader locks out writers and the last reader releases them, so concurrent reads are allowed but writes are exclusive. This solution favors readers, so writers may starve under a continuous stream of readers; a writer-preference variant adds a semaphore read = 1 to block arriving readers once a writer is waiting.
questions.explanation: readcount guarded by mutex lets the first reader block writers and the last reader release them, giving concurrent reads but exclusive writes; reader preference can starve writers.
questions.oneShotPreview: Readers-writers: wrt=1, mutex=1, readcount; 1st reader wait(wrt), last signal(wrt); writers exclusive; reader-preference can starve writers.

questions.q: 8 a) Illustrate Bounded Buffer Problem using semaphore [L3][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: The bounded-buffer problem is the producer-consumer problem for a buffer of finite size n. It is solved with three semaphores: mutex = 1 for mutual exclusion of buffer access, empty = n (number of empty slots), and full = 0 (number of filled slots). Producer: wait(empty) reserves a free slot, wait(mutex) obtains exclusive access, inserts the item, signal(mutex), then signal(full) records a new item. Consumer: wait(full) waits for an item, wait(mutex), removes the item, signal(mutex), then signal(empty) records the freed slot. The empty semaphore prevents writing into a full buffer and full prevents reading from an empty one, while mutex prevents interleaved modification of the buffer. This gives a race-free, busy-wait-free solution; reversing the two waits (taking mutex before empty/full) can deadlock.
questions.explanation: Counting semaphores empty/full track buffer capacity while mutex serializes access — the canonical bounded-buffer solution.
questions.oneShotPreview: Bounded buffer: empty=n, full=0, mutex=1; producer wait(empty)->wait(mutex)->insert->signal(mutex)->signal(full); consumer reverse.

questions.q: 8 b) What is Deadlock? Discuss its system Model and characterization. [L2][CO5] [5M]
questions.a: Deadlock is a permanent blocking state in which a set of processes each hold some resources and wait for additional resources held by other processes in the set, so no member can proceed. System model: the system has a finite set of resource types R1..Rm (e.g., CPU cycles, memory, files, printers), each with a fixed number of identical instances. A process requests a resource via a system call, waits if it is unavailable, uses it, and releases it when done; resources may be reusable (memory, a printer) or consumable (messages, signals). The state is modeled by a resource-allocation graph containing process nodes, resource nodes, and request/assignment edges. Characterization: deadlock exists if and only if all four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously — mutual exclusion (at least one nonsharable resource), hold-and-wait (a process holds resources while waiting for more), no preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and circular wait (a closed chain of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next). A cycle in the graph signals deadlock (necessary and sufficient when each resource has one instance).
questions.explanation: The model views resources as typed, instanced entities; the four Coffman conditions are the necessary and sufficient characterization of deadlock.
questions.oneShotPreview: Deadlock = permanent block; model: finite resources/instances + request/use/release, RAG; characterized by mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.

questions.q: 9 Explain the solutions for Dining-Philosophers Problem. [L2][CO5] [10M]
questions.a: The dining-philosophers problem models five philosophers alternating between thinking and eating, with five chopsticks placed between them; each philosopher needs both adjacent chopsticks to eat, and naively taking one at a time can cause deadlock (everyone holds one and waits for the other) or starvation. Solutions: (1) semaphore/monitor solution — treat each chopstick as a binary semaphore chopstick[5] = 1 and use wait(chopstick[i]) and wait(chopstick[(i+1) mod 5]) before eating and signal on both after; useful but the naive form can deadlock. (2) Break circular wait by asymmetry — odd-numbered philosophers pick left then right, even-numbered ones pick right then left. (3) Allow a philosopher to pick up chopsticks only when both are available, using an atomic double pickup guarded by a mutex. (4) Limit at most four philosophers at the table with a semaphore room = 4, guaranteeing at least one can always eat. (5) Monitor solution with states THINKING, HUNGRY, EATING and condition variables — a philosopher signals neighbors only when both are not eating, avoiding deadlock and ensuring fairness.
questions.explanation: The core problem is circular waiting on shared chopsticks; solutions either break the cycle (ordering, limiting to four) or use atomic pickup/monitor states.
questions.oneShotPreview: Dining philosophers: chopsticks as semaphores; avoid deadlock via odd/even pickup order, atomic both-chopstick pickup, room=4, or monitor with states.

questions.q: 10 a) Suppose there are 2 copies of resource A, 3 copies of resource B, and 3 copies of resource C. Suppose further that process 1 holds one unit of resources B and C and is waiting for a unit of A; that process 2 is holding a unit of A and waiting on a unit of B; and that process 3 is holding one unit of A, two units of B, and one unit of C. (a) Draw the resource allocation graph with description. [L6][CO5] [5M]
questions.a: Allocation state: A has 2 instances, both held (one by P2, one by P3); B has 3 instances, all held (one by P1, two by P3); C has 3 instances, two held (one by P1, one by P3) so one is free. Build the RAG with process nodes P1, P2, P3 (circles) and resource nodes A, B, C (rectangles whose dots show instances). Assignment edges (resource -> process): B -> P1, C -> P1, A -> P2, A -> P3, two edges B -> P3, and C -> P3. Request edges (process -> resource): P1 -> A (P1 waits for A) and P2 -> B (P2 waits for B); P3 has no request edge. Description: P1 holds B and C and requests A; P2 holds A and requests B; P3 holds A, two B and one C and requests nothing. This graph contains the cycle P1 -> A -> P2 -> B -> P1, while P3 is not part of any cycle.
questions.explanation: Mapping holdings to assignment edges and pending requests to request edges reveals the cycle P1-A-P2-B-P1 and shows P3 is outside it.
questions.oneShotPreview: RAG: P1 holds B,C waits A; P2 holds A waits B; P3 holds A,2B,C. Edges show cycle P1->A->P2->B->P1.

questions.q: 10 a) Suppose there are 2 copies of resource A, 3 copies of resource B, and 3 copies of resource C. Process 1 holds one unit of B and C and is waiting for a unit of A; process 2 holds a unit of A and is waiting on a unit of B; process 3 holds one unit of A, two units of B, and one unit of C. (b) Is the system in a deadlocked state? Why or why not? [L6][CO5] [5M]
questions.a: No, the system is not deadlocked. Although the resource-allocation graph contains a cycle (P1 -> A -> P2 -> B -> P1), a cycle is only a sufficient condition for deadlock when every resource type has exactly one instance; here A, B and C have multiple instances. Process P3 has no outstanding request, so it can complete and release its resources (one A, two B and one C). Once P3 releases them, an instance of A becomes free and can be allocated to P1; after P1 finishes it releases its A, B and C, allowing P2 to obtain the B it needs and complete. Because the blocked processes can eventually acquire their needed resources through P3's release, no set of processes is permanently blocked, so there is no deadlock.
questions.explanation: A cycle in a multi-instance RAG is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock; here P3 is outside the cycle and can finish, freeing A and B so P1 and P2 can complete.
questions.oneShotPreview: No deadlock: cycle exists but P3 (no pending requests) can finish, freeing A/B so P1 then P2 complete — cycle not sufficient with multiple instances.

questions.q: 10 b) Describe about Deadlock Prevention Methods. [L2][CO5] [5M]
questions.a: Deadlock prevention ensures that at least one of the four necessary conditions — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — can never hold. Methods: (1) Attack mutual exclusion by making resources sharable wherever possible, e.g., use spooling so a printer appears shared, or allow concurrent read-only file access. (2) Attack hold-and-wait by requiring a process to request and be allocated all the resources it will need at once before it starts (all-or-nothing allocation); the process waits until all are available. (3) Attack no preemption: if a process holding resources requests an unavailable one, its currently held resources are preempted (released) and it must re-request them later; resources may also be preempted from a process that is itself waiting. (4) Attack circular wait by imposing a total ordering (numbering) of all resource types and requiring processes to request resources strictly in increasing order. These methods guarantee deadlock cannot occur, but they can be inefficient — resources may be held idle, concurrency and utilization drop, and some schemes can cause starvation.
questions.explanation: Prevention structurally negates one of the four Coffman conditions; the price is lower resource utilization and possible starvation.
questions.oneShotPreview: Prevention: negate a Coffman condition — share resources, request all at once (no hold-and-wait), preempt, or order resources (no circular wait); safe but lower utilization.

questions.q: 11 Explain the Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance with an example. [L2][CO5] [10M]
questions.a: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance scheme for systems with multiple resource instances. On every request it checks whether granting it would leave the system in a safe state — one in which there exists a safe sequence <P1, P2, ..., Pn> where each process can obtain its remaining needs from the currently available resources plus those released by processes that have already finished. It uses four data structures: Available (free instances per resource type), Max (maximum demand of each process), Allocation (instances currently allocated), and Need = Max - Allocation. When process Pi makes a Request: (1) verify Request <= Need; (2) verify Request <= Available; (3) tentatively grant it (Available -= Request, Allocation += Request, Need -= Request); (4) run the safety algorithm — set Work = Available and Finish = false for all, repeatedly find a process with Need <= Work, mark it finished and add its Allocation to Work; if all processes finish the state is safe and the request is granted, otherwise it is denied and the tentative state is rolled back. Example: in the classic five-process, three-resource system with Available = (3,3,2), a request by P1 for (1,0,2) can be granted because a safe sequence such as <P1, P3, P4, P2, P0> still exists; a request leaving no process executable would be refused.
questions.explanation: By allowing a request only if a safe sequence still exists, the Banker's algorithm guarantees the system never reaches a state from which deadlock is unavoidable.
questions.oneShotPreview: Banker's: grant only if safe state remains; Available/Max/Allocation/Need; request <= Need & Available, tentatively allocate, run safety check; deny if unsafe.
